title: Anthony Albanese to announce huge migration crackdown tomorrow
text:
By NICHOLAS COMINO, POLITICAL REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  10:50 AEST, 16 September 2026   |  Updated:  08:14 AEST, 17 September 2026

432

View  comments

The Albanese government will unveil its long-awaited migration crackdown tomorrow as it seeks to regain control of a key election battleground from One Nation.

Taking a leaf from Pauline Hanson's political playbook, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke will unveil Labor's new migration plan under the dramatic banner: 'Who Arrives, Who Stays, Who Leaves' at the National Press Club tomorrow.

It comes more than a month after his initial appearance was cancelled at the last minute, amid disagreement within cabinet about the extent of the changes.

Since then, the political pressure on Labor over migration has intensified, with One Nation seizing on the issue and unveiling a far more sweeping proposal to slash the temporary migrant population by 750,000 over three years.

Labor is understood to be plotting a sharp reduction in migration, slashing numbers from around 305,000 to 225,000 within two years, after repeatedly overshooting its own forecasts.

To achieve that reduction, the government is reportedly considering tougher deportation efforts for Australia's 77,000 unlawful non-citizens, cuts to partner and backpacker visas, measures to curb visa-hopping and tighter rules around appeals.

The government also wants to rein in the number of bridging visas, which have surged under its watch.

The move follows weeks of mounting pressure on Labor to respond to concerns about record population growth, housing shortages and stretched infrastructure.

Anthony Albanese (pictured) and his government will unveil their new migration laws this week

Tony Burke (pictured) will give a speech titled 'Who Arrives, Who Stays, Who Leaves'

Meanwhile, the coalition is working on its own plan to tie net overseas migration (NOM) to the amount of new homes built, which is currently tracking around 173,000 per year.

Opposition defence spokesman James Paterson said he was looking forward to seeing the detail of Labor's plan, but was 'deeply sceptical about Labor's ability to deliver'.

'Because for four years they've failed to deliver. As for our own policy, we are close to releasing it but we're actually going to do the work to get it right because we are not the government,' he told reporters in Canberra.

'We are seeking to be the government after the next election and we're not going to put out a half-baked policy like One Nation has that hasn't even been costed, the budgetary impacts of which they have no idea.'

Around 1.4 million people have been added to Australia's population through NOM since Labor entered parliament in May 2022.

NOM surged to 538,000 in 2022-23 before easing to 429,000 in 2023-24 and 306,000 in 2024-25. Another 144,000 migrants were added in the second half of 2025.

The government has defended the elevated figures, arguing that not all migration is within the government’s direct control.

'Ministers for immigration don't always have direct levers,' Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen said.

Pauline Hanson (pictured) and One Nation announced their migration policy on Monday

'Quite a lot of our immigration program is demand-driven. If a business needs a temporary skilled worker, then that is something which automatically happens.'

Bowen also pointed to Australians returning from overseas as a significant factor.

'There's things in the total net migration figures to Australia, like Australian residents returning home, as they're perfectly entitled to do,' he said.
